proof.criterion: Review round 2, finding 1 (blocking, measured): the watchdog's select chose between handing a second signal to the drain and exiting by racing two ready channels, so a second signal at a serving broker exited without the drain or srv.Shutdown about 1 run in 150, cutting in-flight requests and logging that the broker had served nothing.
proof.surface: The real compiled binary, serving and healthy, taking two SIGTERMs back to back, repeated; and the decision itself, extracted as secondSignalFindsServing and driven directly rather than through a replica.
proof.command: the decision row: cd packages/envoy && go test -count=1 -run TestASecondSignal -v ./cmd/broker/ ; the binary: a scratch script outside the repository booting the real binary with BROKER_DRAIN_SECONDS=60, waiting for GET /healthz 200, then sending two SIGTERMs a measured gap apart, 300 runs per gap
proof.observed: The watchdog is now again's only reader: it takes both signals and then reads serveStarted once with a select/default, so the branch comes from the state at the instant the second signal arrived. Serving hands the signal to the drain on a new buffered drainNow channel; not serving logs and exits. TestASecondSignalAtAServingBrokerAlwaysDrains asks 500 times with both inputs already ready — the moment a select would coin-flip — and answers drain every time; TestASecondSignalBeforeServingExits is the control. On the real binary: 600 runs across gaps of 80 and 100 microseconds, 354 of them exercising the second signal at a serving broker, runs=300 pass=300 at each gap, every run logging 'broker draining' then 'broker shutting down' and exiting 0.
proof.negativeControl: Both halves are controlled against the old shape, not argued. The decision row run under a go build overlay carrying only the previous body answers 'exit 245 times in 500'. The same binary drive against the pre-change binary at the same gap: runs=300 pass=289 fail=11, each failure exit 1 with 'a second signal arrived while the broker was still starting up, so it is stopping without a drain: it has served nothing' logged straight after 'broker listening' — the reviewer's 2-in-300 replica measurement reproduced at 11-in-300 on the real thing.

proof.criterion: Review round 2, finding 2 (blocking): the reread listener subscribed after the first whole-namespace load, so a narrowing retag a peer served while a pod was loading reached that pod only at its five-minute reload, silently, on every boot — which is what a rolling deploy is. The architect's invariant: the subscription exists before the read whose result it is meant to invalidate.
proof.surface: The two-process harness with the booting pod's store reads fed through a FIFO, which makes the window reproducible from outside: B's first load is given the pre-retag store while A serves the narrowing retag and commits its notification, and only then does B subscribe, catch up and bind.
proof.command: a scratch row added through go test -tags multiprocess -overlay, reusing the two-process harness, -count=10 against the new binary and against the pre-change one
proof.observed: Once OnConnected has fired — so the pod is listening — the boot takes one more whole-namespace load before net.Listen. New binary, 10 of 10 PASS, each 'B's first ask for AUTO_READ_TOKEN, from a session of the old owner: 200 state=pending approver=grace@example.com', so the retag was in force from B's first request. The catch-up runs only when the barrier fired, since with no subscription a second read moves where the window starts rather than closing it, and the timeout branch says so. A failed catch-up does not refuse the boot and logs 'broker: serving without the boot's catch-up policy load, so a retag another pod served while this one was starting may not be in force here until its five-minute reload', deliberately off the 'broker: <operation> failed' shape and given its own row in operate.md's alarm table; a ctx.Err() check follows it as one follows the first load, and stage gains 'the catch-up policy load'.
proof.negativeControl: The same row against the pre-change binary: 10 of 10 FAIL, each '200 state=granted', B serving the tags from before the retag — the lost-notification bug reproduced. The failure path was driven too: with the catch-up's read fed unparseable bytes the boot logs the WARN and carries on to 'broker listening'.

proof.criterion: Review round 2, finding 3 (blocking, Security[secret]): a kind retag's exit 0 is now one pod's answer, while the procedure that reads it as permission to store a long-lived credential was written for a one-pod broker. The architect bounded the fix to one honest sentence in the page this change already edits, and refused a durable fleet-wide fence in advance.
proof.surface: The operator-facing page that gives the procedure, built by the documentation site's own build.
proof.observed: 43 pages built, all internal links valid, exit 0; private names clean over 4905 files. guides/manage-a-secret.md now says, where it tells an operator to store the App key or the Google login once the retag exits 0, that exit 0 is the answer of the one broker process that served the reread and not of every process; names the three ways a peer is left behind with the log line that shows each (the failed notification, a redialing listener, a process still booting); says what a left-behind process does, which is serve the secret as stored for up to five minutes and release its stored value raw to a grant; and gives the two things to do before secret set — read the broker's log for those lines since the retag, and if any names the secret, or the log cannot be read, wait five minutes after exit 0. No fence was built and no kind-transition protocol was added.
proof.negativeControl: One of the three paths is now closed in code rather than documented — the boot window is finding 2's — and the sentence still names it, because a failed catch-up read leaves it open and logs so. That is the honest reading: the page describes what can happen, not what the last release happened to fix.

proof.criterion: The four stale statements swept as a class for the third time on this issue, with the architect's standing rule applied: hold the comment to producing what the code does, since prose is the only thing here no test can pin.
proof.surface: The repository's own text, read against the code above it rather than against the review's list.
proof.command: the documentation build above, plus a read of every comment the diff touches
proof.observed: operate.md's 'more than five secrets at once' reads ten, agreeing with limits.go and with the troubleshooting guide this change had already corrected. AGENTS.md no longer says the bind waits for the 'first dial, successful or not' — it waits for OnConnected, which pglisten runs only once the LISTEN statement has returned — and now carries the catch-up load with it. AGENTS.md no longer says 'a zero drain registers neither': the channel is registered unconditionally before any boot work, one watchdog is its only reader, and a zero drain takes neither the timer nor the select. limits.go credits the other four fifths of the Secret Manager quota to running more pods rather than to the fan-out, since only this route's reread notifies and a miss-path reread, a reload and a release send nothing. packages/envoy/cmd/broker/watchdog_test.go — new: the decision driven 500 times with both inputs ready, and its control
packages/envoy/internal/broker/api/limits.go — the four fifths credited to the replica count rather than to the fan-out
docs/site/src/content/docs/broker/operate.md — the burst figure, and two new alarm-table rows (the catch-up WARN and the second stage value)

packages/envoy/AGENTS.md — the bind's wait and the catch-up load, and the second signal's single reader
trickyParts: The watchdog's decision is a function on purpose: it is the whole of the branch, so a row can drive it with both inputs already ready, which is the only state in which the old shape was wrong. Anyone restoring a select over serveStarted and again reintroduces a 1-in-150 exit in the stop path, and that row is what catches it.

The catch-up load exists to establish an ordering, not to shrink a window: the subscription must predate the read whose result it invalidates. It therefore runs only when OnConnected has fired, and a change that moved it earlier, or made it unconditional, would not mean the same thing.
A kind retag's exit 0 is one pod's answer. The page says so now; the code does not make it a fleet-wide fence, and the architect refused one in advance as a design change smuggled in as a fix.
deviations: One fact recorded in the code as a fact rather than argued, and put to the architect rather than decided here: the catch-up is ordered after the subscription, but its tags come from the store's listing (policy.Loader.Load reads AWS's ListSecrets tags or GCP's ListSecrets annotations), and both stores document listing lag — ListLag is 5 minutes on AWS and 6 hours on GCP. So on a real store the catch-up can read a lagging listing and still show the tags from before a retag a peer made seconds earlier. This separates neither of the two shapes the reviewer named: subscribing before the first load has the same exposure, because a retag committed before any subscription is only ever visible through a listing. The FIFO drive uses the fake store, which has no lag, so it proves the ordering and not freshness against a real store.

The review's cost figure for a namespace load ('one list plus one DescribeSecret per secret') does not match the code: AWS's List is ListSecrets pages plus at most one KMS alias lookup, and GCP's is those pages plus one GetSecretVersion per secret. The comment gives the real figures.

The Postgres this pod ran its tests against was rebuilt during the round: 127.0.0.1:5432 began refusing the test URL and /tmp had been cleared, so a fresh Debian postgresql-17 was extracted and started on 127.0.0.1:55432, and every database-backed check above ran against it.
openQuestions: One, with the architect and not blocking: whether the store's listing lag behind a retag is worth anything beyond the sentence now in the code, given that neither available shape of the fix changes it. It is a property of the stores rather than of this change, and the reviewer has the same text in its thread.
discoveredComplexity: All four stale statements this round came from comments written in the very round that fixed the thing they describe — the pattern the reviewer named for the retro: a person fixing something writes the comment while holding the old behaviour in mind, and nothing rereads it. The check that catches it is reading every comment in a diff against the code above it, which found two more this round that the review had not listed.

A probabilistic defect needs a probabilistic disproof. Finding 1's fix is credible because the same repetition that proved the bug (11 failures in 300 real-binary runs on the old shape) shows none in 600 on the new one; an argument about select would have proved nothing about a 0.7% branch.
